title: The Jesus Prayer
hookLine: one short line, said over and over, moving from the lips toward the heart

cards: A knotted cord of black wool, looped around a wrist. Each knot is tied in a small cross.
An Orthodox Christian moves a thumb from one knot to the next, and with each one says a single line, quietly: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. On a bus. Waiting for coffee.
Lying awake. Just that line, again, until it feels less like something said and more like something breathed. You met this prayer briefly on day one hundred two.
Today, the tradition of stillness it lives in.

teach.b: Hesychasm comes from the Greek hesychia, stillness. It names a way of prayer in Eastern Orthodox Christianity, kept especially by monks, and gathered in a collection of writings called the Philokalia.
First, the words come from the Gospels. In Luke, a tax collector stands far off and prays, in the old King James wording, "God be merciful to me a sinner."
A blind man by the road calls out, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." The Jesus Prayer gathers such cries into one line; some end it with a sinner. Second, the breath.

teach.h: WITH THE BREATH, TOWARD THE HEART.
teach.b: Some writers in the Philokalia describe saying the prayer with the rhythm of breathing, the first half on the in-breath, the second on the out-breath, with the attention resting low, near the heart.
Third, the heart: your line. Orthodox teachers speak of the prayer moving from the lips, to the mind, to the heart, until it becomes the prayer of the heart.
The heart here means the center of the whole person, not just feelings. Fourth, a caution the tradition gives itself.
The breathing methods are a help, not the point, and this prayer is best learned with a spiritual father or mother, not from a book or an app.
For Orthodox Christians this is not a technique for calm; it's speaking to Christ.
So for anyone outside that faith, the respectful way in is to listen and learn, the way you'd sit quietly at the back of someone else's church.

how: Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, often with a knotted prayer rope, repeating it quietly through the day, and monks and others who practice hesychasm learn it under the guidance of a spiritual father or mother.

practice: If you pray as a Christian, you can say the Jesus Prayer slowly, without forcing the breath. If you don't, simply sit in the stillness the word hesychia points to, letting the breath come and go on its own.
Notice where your attention rests in the body, and let it drift down toward the center of the chest.
